stem: A game needs 50 players with the same actions but separate health values. Which design best fits that need?

options.text: One `Player` class and 50 player objects made from it
One health variable shared by every player
Fifty unrelated copies of every function
One object with no class or data

explanation_after: The class holds the shared blueprint, while every object receives its own instance data. That gives all players the same available actions without forcing them to share health.
`self` is the object receiving the method call. Here that object is Mina, so changes to `self.health` change Mina's health rather than every player's health.

stem: Why must a PyTorch model's `__init__` normally call `super().__init__()`?

options.text: It runs `nn.Module`'s setup so layers and parameters can be registered
It converts every input to a tensor

explanation_after: The parent `nn.Module` class has bookkeeping to prepare. Calling its setup lets it notice layers assigned on the child object and later find their trainable parameters.

stem: A `Predictor` uses a separate `Scaler` object to prepare features. What relationship does this show?

options.text: Composition: the predictor has and uses a scaler
Inheritance: the predictor is a kind of scaler

explanation_after: Composition means building an object from collaborating objects. The predictor is not a specialized scaler; it simply contains or receives one and uses its `transform` behavior.

stem: In cooperative multiple inheritance, what does `super().run()` mean?

options.text: Always call the first parent written anywhere in the program
Continue to the next implementation in this object's method resolution order
Call every parent method at the same time
Skip all parent classes and call `object`

explanation_after: `super()` follows the object's MRO. In a cooperative chain, each class does its part and then lets the next class in that ordered route continue.

prompt: Arrange these lines so a `Player` class is defined, an object is created, and that object takes damage.
explanation_after: Define the class first, place the indented method inside it, create an object from the finished class, and only then call the object's method.

prompt: Choose the chip that completes the method: `def rename(self, name): ____ = name`
explanation_after: `self.name` stores the new name on the particular object receiving the method call. A bare local name would disappear when the method ends.
